messages.author: 185f4d4fdb048fb8
messages.subject: Re: Genotyping via oligo? (Was: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: paired analysis)
parts:
Hi,

the quick answer is unfortunately "no", but read more below.

On Thu, Jul 17, 2008 at 3:21 PM, Alex <alex.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Henrik,
>
> Thank you very much for your response, it was extremely useful.
> I was thinking that 6 distinctive log2 ratios on CRL-2324D chr.2 is a
> bit too much, but the contamination would be a likely explanation.
> I would like to ask another question regarding a flow of operation.
> Let's suppose I want to use the aroma.affymetrix raw CN estimation to
> produce the final CN estimation, then use oligo to produce genotype
> calls and then incorporate both CN and genotype calls into the data
> structure accessible through some kind of browser, either
> ChromosomeExplorer or appropriate BioC package (rtracklayer?)

To the best of my understanding, there is not straightforward way to
do this right now. I've focusing on other things than genotyping
lately, so if some knows a way, please let us know.

It is on the todo list to incorporate oligo::CRLMM into the
aroma.affymetrix framework. More than an a year ago, I had a wrapper
for doing this (even to Affymetrix command line BRLMM), but it quickly
became obsolete when oligo evolved.

Benilton Carvalho - the developer/maintainer of oligo - is currently
very busy wrapping up his PhD, but after that is quite keen to do more
work on oligo. My hope is that we then can get a low-level API to
CRLMM that we can hook on to from aroma.affymetrix. With some luck,
maybe we have something working in 2-3 months.

There is no standard way to incorporate genotype tracks into
ChromsomeExplorer. Yet again, I have some alpha/trial code, but
nothing standardized, so don't expect anything. The like solution to
this, is to extend the ChromsomeExplorer to be able to stacks tracks
by using layers and transparent images. I tried to do this for
Firefox 2, but there were too many (for me) uncontrollable memory
leaks in Firefox causing Firefox to stop working after browsing a few
chromosomes. Maybe this has been solved in Firefox 3, which is not
unlikely because they've put a lot into improving the garbage
collector and minimizing the memory overhead. If anyone out there is
a heck-of-a-web2.0 programmer, I would love to have s/he to improve
the current ChromosomeExplorer HTML+Javascript code.

> What would be the strategy to accomplish this? As I understand, oligo
> now runs in bounded memory, so both processing pipelines (aroma and
> oligo) can be launched on a PC, but we are primarily using a Linux
> workstation (32GB +2TB disk space) , so the memory limitations would
> not be a problem.

Yes, memory is less of an issue here.


>
> Thank you,
>
> Alex
>
>
> On Jul 17, 5:05 pm, "Henrik Bengtsson" <h...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
>> Hi Alex,
>>
>>
>>
>> On Thu, Jul 17, 2008 at 1:41 PM, Alex Lisovich <alex.lisov...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> > Dear List,
>>
>> > I am very new to the field of CNV analysis and aroma package so please
>> > forgive me for naive questions.
>> > I am running the paired analysis as described in tutorial. It seems
>> > that there is a typo in paired analysis code sample, specifically in
>> > "PCR fragment length normalization" instead of:
>>
>> > cesFlnList <- list();
>> > for (chipType in names(csList)) {
>> > ces <- cesCnList[[chipType]];
>> > fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces);
>> > print(fln);
>> > cesFln <- process(fln, verbose=log);
>> > cesFlnList[[chipType]] <- cesFln;
>> > }
>>
>> > it should read:
>>
>> > cesFlnList <- list();
>> > for (chipType in names(cesList)) {
>> > ces <- cesList[[chipType]];
>> > fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces);
>> > print(fln);
>> > cesFln <- process(fln, verbose=log);
>> > cesFlnList[[chipType]] <- cesFln;
>> > }
>>
>> > otherwise it will not run due to the name mismatch with the previous
>> > ("Summarization") section.
>>
>> thanks for reporting these typos. The vignette has been updated.
>>
>>
>>
>> > After this fix it works and the result of chr.20 for tumor-normal pair
>> > (CRL-5868D, CRL-5957D) is the same as in the vignette,
>> > but I have the difficulty interpreting the results: it seems that big
>> > chunks of output signal (for example, CRL-2324D vs CRL-2325D, chr.
>> > 1,2,3)
>> > have a shift of a mean value by a fraction of a unity copy number
>> > relative to each other and I am wondering if this a physical or
>> > processing artifact?
>>
>> The first and most important comment is that you cannot and should not
>> interpret the log2 ratios as true/real log2 copy numbers. There are
>> many reasons for this, but one is that the microarray technology does
>> not measure the underlying copy number on a linear (proportional)
>> scale, e.g. if you double the CN the observed signal is not doubled.
>> What holds is that large CNs have large log-ratios and vice verse.
>> This comment applies to all CN data sets.
>>
>> Different methods have been proposed to calibrate the log2 ratios
>> ("raw CNs") toward know CN levels so that can interpret the log2
>> ratios as true log2 ratios. This kind of calibration can be done
>> after normalizing the chip effects (e.g. fragment-length
>> normalization). Doing this kind of calibration will only have little
>> impact on the segmentation, i.e. you will in practice find the same
>> breakpoints in both cases (except maybe for some extremely short noise
>> regions).
>>
>> I don't know the details about this particular data set, but it is
>> quite likely that the tumor sample is contaminated by normal cells as
>> well (very common), which will cause us compare a mixture of tumor and
>> normals towards normals. That would further explain (true) CN levels
>> that are not 0, 1, 2, ... Furthermore, if the tumor sample is not
>> only contaminated by normal cells but also by other kind of tumor
>> cells that have different CN aberrations, you can get very complicated
>> regions.
>>
>> > I've learned from the previous discussions on the list that running
>> > tumor sample against the large enough reference set would remove it
>> > through normalization,. but still what process
>> > would cause such a shift in a paired analysis?
>>
>> Using a large set of pure normals as a reference is only like have a
>> single normal sample with very little noise. The more normals you
>> average over, the less noisy your reference becomes. It does not
>> affect the CN levels of the reference though. It should reflect CN=2
>> at all positions (except possibly for common CN polymorphic regions).
>> Having a small number of normals in the reference will typically just
>> add noise, but it is unlikely that it will "introduce" CN regions.
>>
>> > I thought that
>> > neighboring SNPs are scattered across the chip so it should not be a
>> > local chip luminance variance.
>>
>> Each SNP contain multiple probes (except the single CN probes on the
>> newer arrays). These probes are never placed close to each other.
>> Instead they are spread out spatially on the array to minimize the
>> risk that one SNP will be biased by spatial artifacts. Furthermore,
>> neighboring SNPs on the genome are not placed next to each other on
>> the array. I don't know if Affymetrix have done a randomization for
>> this explicitly, but their standard probe position algorithm is likely
>> to introduce such a "semi-randomization".
>>
>> > I would greatly appreciate a brief explanation of this phenomenon.
>>
>> Hope this helps. If not, I suggest that you continue this
>> non-aroma.affymetrix specific question on Bioconductor where more
>> people can pitch in.
>>
>> Cheers
>>
>> Henrik
>>
>>
>>
>> > Thank you
>>
>> > Alex Lisovich
>> > University of Pittsburgh, DBMI
>> > 200 Meyran Ave
> >
>

parts:
Dear Henrik,

Thank you very much for explaining the current status-quo.
Unfortunately, I never wrote web applications, only signal/image
processing in C/C++, Java, Matlab and GUI in Java and C++/QT/MSVC

Let me describe our situation: our lab recently run a set of 500k
samples which where acquired under worst circumstances
possible: the samples are all brain tumors taken during surgery,
they are all paraffin embedded (FFPE), there is no normal FFPE
references ,
and the normal DNA contamination is extremely high.

As a result, the SD of raw CN is about 4 times higher than normal
when
HapMap ref. set is used (compared to Affy tumor-normal set)
and the change in CN for gain/loss regions is a small fraction of CN
unity.
For that reason, all HMM based packages I tried (Affy, CNAG, dCHip)
produced un-interpretable results which change quite unpredictably
with settings tweaking. From the other hand aroma.affymetrix
does the segmentation (CBS) which produces sensible
results being based on first principles.

The problem is that I am planning to use Bayesian networks for
downstream classification (among other methods) which requires the
discrete input parameters, hence transforming to "virtual" CN=0,1...N
is disirable.
I understand that it's possible to use getRegions()/writeRegions() to
produce
tab delimited files and start from here, but this would mean no
processing pipeline,
besides CBS in aroma.affymetrix happily continues the segment
over the non-existing regions with negative signals, even if these
regions are large,
hence some condition for region interruption is needed.
So it seems the best way to proceed is to work with source code and
try to incorporate mergeLevels
and subsequent ranking into aroma.affymetrix to start with. Besides,
other people would also benefit from this attempt if it will work.

I noticed that you provide the source code under the private license.
Is it possible to obtain such a license provided that we are in the
academic institution (Univ. of Pittsburgh) and what the terms and
conditions of such
license would be?

Thank you,

Alex Lisovich

Yes, contributions are most welcome and the more we share
algorithms/implementations the more we can focus on the biological
science. Contributions can be done either as 3rd party plugin
packages or possible part of the aroma.affymetrix package itself.

>
> I noticed that you provide the source code under the private license.
> Is it possible to obtain such a license provided that we are in the
> academic institution (Univ. of Pittsburgh) and what the terms and
> conditions of such
> license would be?

When I first went public with aroma.affymetrix I put it under "private
license" because I couldn't decide on which of the GPL, LPGL, Artistic
etc licenses is the best for everyone. So the intention is to choose
an open source license whenever I get around to really read up on the
details.

To answer your immediate needs, as an academic institution, feel free
to go ahead as use it as if it is under GPL, put don't redistribute it
(if you need that) under that license until I've settled it.

Cheers

Henrik

>> >> Each SNP contain multiple probes (except the single CN probes on the

>> >> risk that one SNP will be biased by spatial artifacts. Furthermore,

>> >> the array. I don't know if Affymetrix have done a randomization for
>> >> this explicitly, but their standard probe position algorithm is likely
>> >> to introduce such a "semi-randomization".
